In what year was Empress Elisabeth of Austria born?
Empress Elisabeth of Austria: Elisabeth was born into the Bavarian House of Wittelsbach but enjoyed an informal upbringing before marrying her first cousin, Emperor Franz Joseph I, at 16.
In what year was Ron DeSantis born?
Ron DeSantis: Ronald Dion DeSantis (born September 14, 1978) is an American politician, attorney, and former naval officer serving as the 46th governor of Florida since 2019.
In what year was Edward VIII born?
Edward VIII: Edward was born during the reign of his great-grandmother Queen Victoria as the eldest child of the Duke and Duchess of York, later King George V and Queen Mary.
In what year was Diana, Princess of Wales born?
Diana, Princess of Wales (born Diana Frances Spencer; 1 July 1961 – 31 August 1997), was a member of the British royal family.
In what year did George V die?
George V: From 1877 to 1892, George served in the Royal Navy, until his elder brother's unexpected death in January 1892 put him directly in line for the throne.
In what year did Bernard Tapie die?
Bernard Tapie: Bernard Roger Tapie (French: [bɛʁnaʁ ʁɔʒe tapi]; 26 January 1943 – 3 October 2021) was a French businessman, politician and occasional actor, singer, and TV host.
In what year was Muslim Brotherhood founded?
Muslim Brotherhood: The group later advanced into the political arena, aiming to end British colonial rule in Egypt.
In what year was Government of India founded?
Government of India: India is a parliamentary republic led by the president of India who, as the ceremonial head of state, holds formal executive power.
In what year was Interpol founded?
Interpol: It is the world's largest international police organization.
Safavid dynasty: Ismail I. The Safavid dynasty had its origin in the Safavid Sufi order, which was established in the city of Ardabil in the Iranian Azerbaijan region.
Whig Party (United States): Henry Clay. The Whig Party was a political party in the United States that existed from 1833 to 1856.
Taoism: Laozi. Taoism or Daoism is a philosophical and religious tradition indigenous to China, emphasizing harmony with the Tao 道.
In which country did the Battle of Rorke's Drift take place?
Battle of Rorke's Drift: Zulu Kingdom. The Battle of Rorke's Drift, also known as the Defence of Rorke's Drift, was an engagement in the Anglo-Zulu War.
In which country was the Western Chalukya Empire?
Western Chalukya Empire: India. The Western Chalukya Empire ( chə-LOO-kyə) ruled most of the western Deccan, South India, between the 10th and 12th centuries.
Holodomor: Soviet Union. The Holodomor, also known as the Ukrainian famine, was a massive man-made famine in Soviet Ukraine from 1932 to 1933 that killed millions of Ukrainians.
In which country was the Portuguese Empire?
Portuguese Empire: Kingdom of Portugal. The Portuguese Empire, c. 1415 to 1999, was the first and longest lasting of the European colonial empires.
In which country did the Mukden incident take place?
Mukden incident: Republic of China. The Mukden incident was a false flag event staged by Japanese military personnel as a pretext for the 1931 Japanese invasion of Manchuria.
In which country is Union Public Service Commission based?
Union Public Service Commission: India. The agency's charter is granted by Part XIV of the Constitution of India, titled Services Under the Union and the States.
In which country is Loch Ness Monster?
Loch Ness Monster: United Kingdom. It is often described as large, long-necked, and with one or more humps protruding from the water.
In which country did the 2019 El Paso Walmart shooting take place?
2019 El Paso Walmart shooting: United States. On August 3, 2019, a mass shooting occurred at a Walmart store in El Paso, Texas, United States.
In which country was Chera dynasty?
Chera dynasty: India. The Chera country was geographically well placed at the tip of the Indian peninsula to profit from maritime trade via the extensive Indian Ocean networks.
Which of these was an official language of the Sultanate of Zanzibar?
Sultanate of Zanzibar: Swahili. It was also involved in the shortest war in history, the Anglo-Zanzibar War, which lasted 38 minutes on the morning of 27 August 1896.
Which of these was an official language of the Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria?
Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria: German. It maintained a degree of provincial autonomy, and its status remained unchanged until the dissolution of the monarchy in 1918.
Which of these was an official language of Denmark–Norway?
Denmark–Norway: Danish. The state also claimed sovereignty over three historical peoples: Frisians, Gutes and Wends.
Which country used the grivna as its official currency?
The grivna is the official currency of Novgorod Republic. For much of its history, Novgorod was the center of Russian art and culture.
This messianic movement arose in British India in the late 19th century after its founder declared himself the promised Messiah and Mahdi — what movement is it?
Ahmadiyya is an Islamic messianic movement originating in British India in the late 19th century.
The longest-serving Home Affairs Minister in Indian history, this politician also led the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party as its president from 2014 to 2020 — who is he?
Amit Shah (born 22 October 1964) is an Indian politician who has served as the 31st Minister of Home Affairs since 2019, the longest-serving holder of the office in Indian history.

This 19th-century Habsburg-Lorraine royal fathered two emperors — one who ruled from Vienna, the other who ruled Mexico — and was grandfather to the royal whose 1914 assassination triggered World War I — who is he?
Archduke Franz Karl of Austria (17 December 1802 - 8 March 1878) was a member of the House of Habsburg-Lorraine.
Fought in southern Anatolia on 5 November 333 BC, this clash saw Alexander the Great rout Darius III, who fled leaving behind his family and treasury — which engagement was it?
Battle of Issus (also Issos) occurred in southern Anatolia, on 5 November 333 BC between the Hellenic League led by Alexander the Great and the Achaemenid (or Persian) Empire, led by Darius III.
Widow of King Prasutagus, which queen of the Iceni tribe led a failed revolt against Roman occupation of Britain around AD 60?

An Argentine Marxist revolutionary whose stylized image became a countercultural icon of rebellion, he was horrified by poverty and inequality while traveling as a medical student. His involvement in Guatemala's social reforms led him to become a major figure of which revolution?
Che Guevara (14 June 1928 - 9 October 1967) was an Argentine Marxist revolutionary, author, guerrilla leader, diplomat, politician, and military theorist.
This Swedish diplomat became the youngest person ever elected UN Secretary-General at just 47, serving from 1953 until his death in a 1961 plane crash — who is he?

Dag Hammarskjöld (29 July 1905 - 18 September 1961) was a Swedish economist and diplomat who served as the second Secretary-General of the United Nations from April 1953 until his death in a plane crash in September 1961.
Nominated three times for the Medal of Honor and finally awarded it for his WWII service in the Philippines, this American general also served as Army chief of staff in the 1930s. Who is he?
Douglas MacArthur (26 January 1880 - 5 April 1964) was an American general who served as a top commander during World War II and the Korean War, achieving the rank of General of the Army.

A World War I officer decorated with the Pour le Mérite, he later wrote the tactics classic 'Infantry Attacks' and commanded the 7th Panzer Division — though history remembers him as 'The Desert Fox.' Who was he?
Erwin Rommel (15 November 1891 - 14 October 1944), known as The Desert Fox, was a German Generalfeldmarschall (field marshal) during World War II.
This Norse goddess of love, beauty, and war owns a magical necklace called Brísingamen, rides a chariot pulled by two cats, and can transform into a falcon using an enchanted cloak — who is she?
Freyja (Old Norse '(the) Lady') is a goddess associated with love, beauty, fertility, sex, war, gold, and seir (magic for seeing and influencing the future).
Founded in 918, this Korean kingdom achieved what historians call the peninsula's first true national unification, ruling until the Joseon dynasty was established in 1392 — what kingdom was it?

Goryeo (Middle) was a Korean state founded in 918, during a time of national division called the Later Three Kingdoms period, that unified and ruled the Korean Peninsula until the establishment of Joseon in 1392.
Often depicted holding twin torches or a key, or accompanied by dogs, this Greek goddess of crossroads, magic, and witchcraft first appeared in Hesiod's Theogony in the 8th century BCE — who is she?

Hecate (Ancient) is a goddess in ancient Greek religion and mythology, most often shown holding a pair of torches, a key, or snakes, or accompanied by dogs, and in later periods depicted as three-formed or triple-bodied.

Descended from a Welsh noble family and Catherine of Valois, this English and Welsh royal dynasty held the throne from 1485 to 1603 across five monarchs including Henry VIII and Elizabeth I — name the dynasty?
House of Tudor was an English and Welsh dynasty that held the throne of England from 1485 to 1603.
This Israeli far-right politician has served as minister of national security since 2022 and leads a Kahanist party called 'Jewish Power.' Who is he?
Itamar Ben-Gvir (born 6 May 1976) is an Israeli politician and lawyer who has served as the minister of national security since 2022, except for a two-month gap in early 2025.
This California politician served two non-consecutive stints as governor decades apart, making him both the state's oldest and, at the time, its sixth-youngest governor — who is he?
Jerry Brown (born April 7, 1938) is an American lawyer, author, and politician who served as the 34th and 39th governor of California from 1975 to 1983 and 2011 to 2019.
Overthrown in 1955 yet returned to Argentina's presidency in 1973, this military-college graduate gave his name to a political force still shaping the country — who?

Juan Perón (8 October 1895 - 1 July 1974) was an Argentine military officer and politician who was the 29th and 40th president of Argentina, serving from 1946 to his overthrow in 1955, and from 1973 until his death in 1974.

Founded around 1000 AD when Stephen I was crowned its first king, this Central European monarchy — later split by Ottoman occupation into three parts — endured for nearly a millennium until 1946. What was it?
Kingdom of Hungary was a monarchy in Central Europe that existed for nearly a millennium, from 1000 to 1946.

This US Army officer served with the 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment of the 101st Airborne during World War II, and was portrayed by Ron Livingston in the HBO miniseries Band of Brothers — who is he?

Lewis Nixon III (September 30, 1918 - January 11, 1995) was a United States Army officer who, during World War II, served at the company, battalion, and regimental level with the 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment, 101st Airborne Division.

Quoted by Jesus in 'You cannot serve both God and ___,' this New Testament word for wealth was later personified in medieval tradition as one of the seven princes of Hell, representing greed — what's the word?
Mammon is commonly thought to mean money, material wealth, or any entity that promises wealth, and is associated with the greedy pursuit of gain.
This American memoirist and poet's first of seven autobiographies, published in 1969, told of her life up to age 17 and brought her international recognition. Who is she?
Maya Angelou (born Marguerite Annie Johnson; April 4, 1928 - May 28, 2014) was an American memoirist, essayist, poet, and civil rights activist.
Known as "The Proclamator," this independence activist was once jailed in the Boven Digoel concentration camp before becoming his country's very first vice president. Who was he?

Mohammad Hatta (n Athar; 12 August 1902 - 14 March 1980) was an Indonesian statesman, nationalist, and independence activist who served as the country's first vice president as well as the third prime minister.

Most often used as an insult and rarely pinned to one clear definition, this late-20th-century ideology champions free-market capitalism through lower taxes, privatization and deregulation — what is it called?
Neoliberalism is a political and economic ideology that advocates for free-market capitalism, which became dominant in policy-making from the late 20th century onward.
According to Genesis, this second son of Judah defied the custom of levirate marriage with his brother Er's widow, Tamar, and was punished for it — who was he?
Onan was a figure detailed in the Book of Genesis chapter 38, as the second son of Judah and his Canaanite wife, the daughter of Shuah.
This Confucian scholar-turned-revolutionary led rebel armies against French colonial forces in 19th-century Vietnam, refusing to surrender even after they desecrated his ancestral tombs. Who was he?
Phan Đình Phùng (1847 - January 21, 1896) was a Vietnamese revolutionary who led rebel armies against French colonial forces in Vietnam.
Born in 1988, this Indian politician served as an MLA from Delhi's Rajinder Nagar before joining the Rajya Sabha in 2022 and later switching parties to the BJP — who is he?
Raghav Chadha (born 11 November 1988) is an Indian politician and chartered accountant who serves as a Member of Parliament in the Rajya Sabha since 2022.

Rising to major general by 1979, this South Korean army officer backed his military academy friend's coup that year and later became, in 1987, the first president chosen by direct popular vote. Who is he?
Roh Tae-woo (4 December 1932 - 26 October 2021) was a South Korean army general and politician who served as the sixth president of South Korea from 1988 to 1993.

This Indian politician served as governor of five different states — including Jammu and Kashmir — after earlier representing Aligarh in the national parliament as a member of the Janata Dal. Who is he?

Satya Pal Malik (24 July 1946 - 5 August 2025) was an Indian politician, lawyer and statesman who served as governor of five Indian states, namely Bihar, Odisha, Jammu and Kashmir, Goa, and Meghalaya.
Educated in the United States before marrying revolutionary leader Sun Yat-sen in 1915, she was later named Honorary Chairman of the People's Republic just before her death in 1981 — who was she?
Soong Ching-ling (27 January 1893 - 29 May 1981; Christian name Rosamonde or Rosamond) was a Chinese politician.
Under this Roman power-sharing system, the roles of augustus and caesar were likened to Jupiter and his son Hercules, and it endured from 293 to 324 — what was it called?

Tetrarchy was the system instituted by Roman emperor Diocletian to govern the ancient Roman Empire by dividing it between two emperors, the augusti, and their junior colleagues and designated successors, the caesares.

This German admiral led the Abwehr military intelligence service from 1935 to 1944, and despite initially supporting Hitler, turned to acts of resistance against the Nazi regime after the invasion of Poland — who was he?
Wilhelm Canaris (1 January 1887 - 9 April 1945) was a German admiral and the chief of the Abwehr (the German military-intelligence service) from 1935 to 1944.

A close associate of Mahatma Gandhi and a founding member of the Jamia Millia Islamia university, this Hyderabad-born educationist rose to serve as president of India from 1967 until his death two years later — who was he?

Zakir Husain (8 February 1897 - 3 May 1969) was an Indian educationist and politician who served as the vice president of India from 1962 to 1967 and president of India from 13 May 1967 until his death on 3 May 1969.

Born in a one-room log cabin and self-educated, this lawyer became a leader of a new political party after being angered by the Kansas-Nebraska Act, won a Senate campaign famous for its debates, and then led a nation through its bloodiest conflict. Who was the 16th U.S. president?
Abraham Lincoln: President of the United States from 1861 to 1865.
Regarded by modern historians as the true founder of the Abbasid Caliphate, this caliph also founded the 'Round City' of Madinat al-Salam that became the heart of imperial Baghdad — who was he?
Cousin and son-in-law of the prophet Muhammad, he became the fourth Rashidun caliph and is revered as the first Shia Imam before his assassination in 661 — who is he?
Ali: 1st Shia Imam and 4th Rashidun caliph (656–661)
This Polish farmer-turned-politician founded an agrarian populist party in 1992 known for blockading roads, then briefly served as Deputy Prime Minister in a 2006 coalition government — who is he?
As India's finance minister from 2014 to 2019, this politician oversaw the rollout of the GST and the merger of the railway budget with the general budget — who is he?
Arun Jaitley: Indian politician and attorney (1952–2019)
Leader of the Hitler Youth from 1931 to 1940 and later Nazi governor of Vienna, this German politician was elected to the Reichstag in 1932 — who was he?
Baldur von Schirach: German Nazi politician (1907–1974)
The only British prime minister born Jewish, this Conservative statesman clashed repeatedly with Liberal rival William Gladstone — who is he?
Benjamin Disraeli: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom (1868; 1874–1880)
Sometimes called the Japanese Revolution, this 1868–69 civil war pitted the ruling Tokugawa shogunate against samurai of Chōshū and Satsuma fighting in the emperor's name — what was it called?
Boshin War: 1868–1869 Japanese civil war. When the Boshin War began, Japan was already modernizing, following the same course of advancement as that of the industrialized Western nations.
Cursed by Apollo to speak true prophecies that no one would ever believe, this Trojan priestess survived the fall of Troy only to be murdered alongside Agamemnon. Who was she?
Cassandra: Mythological prophetess and princess of Troy.
Crowned king of the Franks as an infant under his mother Fredegund's regency, he pursued her feud with Queen Brunhilda to a brutal end — her execution by dismemberment in 613. Which king?

Famous for a lifelong lack of interest in politics and war, this Byzantine emperor — long overshadowed as co-ruler before finally reigning alone — held the throne for 66 years, the longest of any Roman emperor since Augustus — who was he?
Constantine VIII: Byzantine emperor from 962 to 1028.
Styled Earl of Rocksavage before inheriting his title, this British peer and filmmaker served as Lord Great Chamberlain of England for over three decades — who is he?
David Cholmondeley, 7th Marquess of Cholmondeley: British filmmaker (born 1960)
Which Indian politician, a granddaughter of Jaipur's last ruling Maharaja, became Deputy Chief Minister of Rajasthan in December 2023?
Diya Kumari: 6th Deputy Chief Minister of Rajasthan. Kumari is the granddaughter of Man Singh II, the last ruling Maharaja of the princely state of Jaipur during the British Raj in India.
A central figure in the Wars of the Roses, this Yorkist king won the throne after victories at Mortimer's Cross and Towton, lost it in 1470, then regained it in 1471 — who is it?
Known by his initials EPN, this PRI politician went from Governor of the State of Mexico to the nation's presidency, serving from 2012 to 2018 — who is he?
Enrique Peña Nieto: President of Mexico from 2012 to 2018. Born in Atlacomulco and raised in Toluca, Peña Nieto attended Panamerican University, graduating with a B.A. in legal studies.

Suppressed by Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government and sparked by resentment toward corrupt post-1945 rule, this 1947 Taiwanese uprising became a key catalyst for the island's independence movement — what's it called?
February 28 incident: 1947 uprising in Taiwan. Directed by provincial governor Chen Yi and president Chiang Kai-shek, thousands of civilians were killed beginning on February 28.
Serving as Foreign Minister in the 1820s, this royalist French writer and diplomat later had his memoirs published posthumously as 'Memoirs from Beyond the Grave' — who was he?
François-René de Chateaubriand: French writer, politician and historian (1768–1848)
This West Point graduate became Commanding General of the U.S. Army early in the Civil War, then ran as the Democratic candidate who lost the 1864 presidential election. Who was he?
George B. McClellan: American major general (1826–1885)

This Germanic people, first recorded by Greco-Roman writers in the 3rd century near the Lower Danube, played a major role in toppling the Western Roman Empire after being pushed west by the Huns — who were they?
Goths: Early Germanic people. The Goths were a Germanic people who played a major role in the fall of the Western Roman Empire and the emergence of medieval Europe.
Raised in Brooklyn's Crown Heights, this Democratic congressman succeeded Nancy Pelosi to become House minority leader in 2023 — who is he?

In faiths with a linear history this afterlife place can be eternal, while reincarnation-based religions treat it as merely a stop between lives — and it's often imagined beneath the Earth's surface; what is it?
Hell: Abode of the dead, in various cultures.
Legend holds this samurai general never took a single wound across 57 military campaigns serving Tokugawa Ieyasu — which of the 'Four Heavenly Kings' is it?
Honda Tadakatsu: 16th-Century AD Japanese samurai, general and daimyo.

A Zaghawa commander who helped win the "Toyota War," he was purged and exiled to Libya, then stormed back to seize power — and ruled Chad for 30 years until he was killed during a 2021 offensive. Who was this longest-serving Chadian president?
Idriss Déby: President of Chad from 1990 to 2021.

Formed in 1946 by former supporters of Benito Mussolini's Republican Fascist Party, which political party became postwar Italy's fourth-largest by the early 1960s while presenting itself as the defender of fascism's legacy?
Italian Social Movement: Neo-fascist political party, 1946–1955.
Founded in July 1999 by former Indian prime minister H. D. Deve Gowda as a breakaway faction, this party is recognized as a state party in Karnataka — which one?
Janata Dal (Secular): State political party in India.

Serving as U.S. Special Envoy for Northern Ireland from 2022 to 2024, this Massachusetts congressman is also the grandson of a senator and attorney general and grandnephew of a president assassinated in 1963 — who is he?

In 1900 he published the best-seller "Sailing Alone Around the World," recounting how he became the first person to circle the globe single-handed — before vanishing at sea aboard his boat the Spray in 1909. Who was he?
Joshua Slocum: 19th-century Canadian-American seaman; first to circumnavigate the world solo.

Grandson of the last Austro-Hungarian emperor, this pro-European former member of the European Parliament has devoted his career to protecting cultural heritage from war and disaster — who heads this once-ruling dynasty?

Ruled by a monarch called the Manikongo, this Central African state at its peak stretched from the Atlantic coast to the Kwango River and lasted as an independent power from around 1390 to 1862 — which realm?
Kingdom of Kongo: 1390–1914 state in Central Africa; Portuguese vassal from 1857.
Once a shoemaker before joining the Bolsheviks in 1911, this close associate of Stalin rose to the Politburo in 1930 after helping consolidate Soviet power across Ukraine and Turkestan — who is he?
A maternal uncle of Prince Philip, this naval officer became the last Viceroy of India and oversaw its transition to independence — by what title is he commonly known?
Lord Mountbatten: British statesman and admiral (1900–1979)
Central to the rise of both Jainism and Buddhism, which ancient Indian kingdom in the eastern Ganges Plain formed the core of the Mauryan and Gupta empires?
Magadha: Region and Mahajanapada in ancient eastern India.
She became heir to Denmark's throne only after a 1953 amendment let women inherit, then reigned exactly 52 years before abdicating in 2024 — which queen?
Margrethe II: Queen of Denmark from 1972 to 2024.
A radical Jacobin lawyer-turned-revolutionary, he championed universal male suffrage and served on the Committee of Public Safety before meeting a grim end in 1794. Who?
Maximilien Robespierre: French revolutionary, lawyer and politician (1758–1794)
Plucked from running Russia's Federal Taxation Service, this economist was confirmed as prime minister in a single day in January 2020 after the entire previous government resigned — who is it?
Mikhail Mishustin: Russian politician and economist (born 1966)
Hidden by his mother among the bulrushes of the Nile as a baby, this prophet grew up to lead the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt. Who is he?
After two failed attempts in 1944, this Hindu nationalist activist shot Mahatma Gandhi three times at a Delhi prayer meeting in January 1948 — who was he?
Nathuram Godse: Assassin of Mahatma Gandhi (1910–1949)
Trained as a classical ballet instructor and educated in Czechoslovakia, this monarch ascended the Cambodian throne in 2004, just a week after his father's abdication — who is he?
Norodom Sihamoni: King of Cambodia since 2004.
This Austrian-born SS commando led the Gran Sasso raid that freed Mussolini from captivity and later advised Egypt's Gamal Abdel Nasser after fleeing to Franco's Spain — who was he?
This British explorer and his eldest son vanished in 1925 hunting an ancient lost city he was convinced lay hidden in the Amazon rainforest — who was he?
Percy Fawcett: British explorer and military officer.
Begun when reformer Alexander Dubček became First Secretary in January 1968, this period of liberalization in Czechoslovakia ended with a Warsaw Pact invasion that August — what is it called?

Prague Spring: Liberalisation in Czechoslovakia in 1968. The Prague Spring (Czech: Pražské jaro; Slovak: Pražská jar) was a period of political liberalization and mass protest in 
the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic.
This Indian politician became Minister of Defence in 2019 and was the first person born after independence to serve as Union Minister of Home Affairs — who is he?
Rajnath Singh: Defense Minister of India since 2019.
Going by his initials 'rms,' this programmer launched the GNU Project, founded the Free Software Foundation, and wrote every version of the GNU General Public License — who is he?
Richard Stallman: American activist and programmer (born 1953)
Orphaned of his murdered father at age two, this Shia cleric grew up to lead a revolution that toppled the Shah and made him his country's first supreme leader — who was he?
Ruhollah Khomeini: Supreme Leader of Iran from 1979 to 1989.
Inspired by a 4th-century Greek bishop known for secret gift-giving, this white-bearded, red-suited figure is said to deliver presents by sleigh on Christmas Eve — who is he?

Santa Claus: Legendary Christmas figure. Santa Claus is a legendary figure originating in Western Christian culture who is said to bring gifts during the late evening and overnight hours on Christmas Eve.
The longest-serving president in his country's republican history, this Italian statesman has held office since 2015 and helped found the Democratic Party in 2007 — who is he?
Sergio Mattarella: President of Italy since 2015. Sergio Mattarella (born 23 July 1941) is an Italian politician who has been serving as the president of Italy since 2015.
Existing from 57 BCE to 935 CE and forming the Three Kingdoms of Korea alongside Paekche and Goguryeo, which kingdom had the smallest population of the three?
Silla: Korean kingdom (57 BCE–935 CE). Silla was one of the longest-lasting countries in Korean history.
Writing under the pseudonym 'Frank Talk,' this South African activist led the grassroots Black Consciousness Movement against apartheid in the late 1960s and 1970s — who is he?
Thomas Seymour, 1st Baron Seymour of Sudeley
Steve Biko: South African anti-apartheid activist (1946–1977)

As senior counselor to a Tokugawa shōgun, this Edo-period official pursued reforms that debased the currency and sold monopoly rights to merchants — remembered for both economic innovation and rampant corruption — who was he?
Tanuma Okitsugu: Japanese political advisor, rōjū (1719–1788)

Named as a single people by the ancient Greeks, this Indo-European group inhabited modern Bulgaria, Romania, and parts of Greece and Turkey, giving rise to tribes like the Getae and Dacians — who were they?
Thracians: Indo-European people in ancient southeast Europe.
Once an actor who ran the film company Red Giant Movies, he served as Tamil Nadu's Deputy Chief Minister from 2024 to 2026 before becoming the state's Opposition Leader. Who is he?
Udhayanidhi Stalin: Indian politician and former actor.
In 1976, this Soviet pilot defected to the West by flying his MiG-25 'Foxbat' jet interceptor to Japan, handing the CIA what George H. W. Bush called an 'intelligence bonanza' — who is he?
Viktor Belenko: Soviet pilot who defected to the West (1947–2023)
One of the most popular presidents at his death in 1923, this Ohio newspaperman who built up the Marion Star saw his reputation later wrecked by exposed scandals — who was he?
Warren G. Harding: President of the United States from 1921 to 1923.
Raging from 1914 to 1918 and nicknamed 'the Great War,' this conflict's mass troop movements helped spread the deadly Spanish flu pandemic — which war?
World War I: 1914–1918 global conflict. The war saw important developments in weaponry including tanks, aircraft, artillery, machine guns, and chemical weapons.
This late-Qing statesman raised and organized the Xiang Army to crush the Taiping Rebellion and helped launch the Tongzhi Restoration — who was he?
Zeng Guofan: Chinese politician and military commander (1811–1872)
Which one below was born first?
John Ray (born 1627) is the earliest of the four. John Ray (29 November 1627 – 17 January 1705) was an English Christian naturalist and one of the earliest English parson-naturalists.
Which of these four was born earliest?

Ivan Pavlov (born 1849) is the earliest of the four. Pavlov also conducted significant research on the physiology of digestion, for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1904.
Pascal (programming language) (founded 1970) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
SQL (founded 1974) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as an astronomer?
Pope Sylvester II is an astronomer.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
Blaise Pascal is a mathematician. Blaise Pascal (19 June 1623 – 19 August 1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer.
What is the atomic number of Dubnium?
Dubnium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Db and atomic number 105.
What is the atomic number of Iridium?
Iridium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ir and atomic number 77.
In what year did Pope Benedict XVI die?
Pope Benedict XVI: Following his resignation, he chose to be known as "pope emeritus", a title he held until his death on 31 December 2022.
In what year was Helium discovered?
Helium: Helium (from Ancient Greek: ἥλιος, romanized: helios, lit. 'sun') is a chemical element; it has symbol He and atomic number 2.
Mil Mi-24: Mil Moscow Helicopter Plant. It is produced by Mil Moscow Helicopter Plant and was introduced by the Soviet Air Force in 1972.
Which country is General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon from?
General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon: United States. The aircraft was first developed by General Dynamics in 1974.
Who is credited with discovering Pyxis?
Pyxis: Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. Pyxis is a small and faint constellation in the southern sky.
Who is credited with discovering Neodymium?
Neodymium: Carl Auer von Welsbach. Neodymium is a chemical element; it has symbol Nd and atomic number 60.
Who is credited with discovering TON 618?
Who is credited with discovering Thallium?
Thallium: Claude-Auguste Lamy. Thallium is a chemical element; it has symbol Tl and atomic number 81.

This Scottish physician's 1928 discovery of a mould-derived substance later named benzylpenicillin has been called the single greatest victory ever achieved over disease, and earned him a shared Nobel Prize in 1945 — who is he?
Alexander Fleming (6 August 1881 - 11 March 1955) was a Scottish physician and microbiologist.
Dating back to the Neolithic Revolution around 13,000 BC, this branch of agriculture covers the breeding, feeding, and day-to-day care of livestock raised for meat, milk, or fiber — what's it called?
Animal husbandry is the branch of agriculture concerned with animals that are raised for meat, fibre, milk, or other products.
Named from Greek words for 'even' and 'toe,' this mammal order bears its weight equally on two of its five toes, unlike its odd-toed counterpart — what order is it?
Artiodactyla (from Ancient Greek rtios 'even' and dktylos 'finger, toe') is an order of placental mammals.

Ranking among the largest wild cats, this population of the Panthera tigris tigris subspecies has roamed the Indian subcontinent since the Late Pleistocene and is found from India to southwestern China — name it?
Bengal tiger is a population of the Panthera tigris tigris subspecies. It is distributed from India, southern Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan to Southwestern China.
Native to the Mediterranean and also called 'starflower,' this annual herb's seeds are pressed for oil even though the plant carries mild toxic alkaloids — which plant?
Borage (or; Borago officinalis), also known as starflower, is an annual herb in the flowering plant family Boraginaceae native to the Mediterranean region.

Native to the Philippines and nearby Southeast Asia, this small sour citrus fruit — a natural hybrid of kumquat and mandarin — flavors everything from marinades to beverages in Filipino cooking — which fruit?
Calamansi (Citrus microcarpa), also known as calamondin, Philippine lime, or Philippine lemon, is a citrus hybrid cultivated predominantly in the Philippines.
A first-generation cephalosporin that can be swallowed rather than infused, this antibiotic disrupts the bacterial cell wall to treat ear, skin and urinary infections — what is it?
Cefalexin is an antibiotic that can treat a number of bacterial infections. It kills gram-positive and some gram-negative bacteria by disrupting the growth of the bacterial cell wall.
Resembling an oversized lemon with a thick, coarse rind, this large fragrant citrus fruit is one of the original ancestors from which all other citrus varieties developed — which fruit?

Citron (Citrus medica) is a large fragrant citrus fruit with a thick, coarse rind. It is one of the original citrus fruits from which all other citrus types developed through natural hybrid speciation or artificial hybridization.

Forming colonies of thousands of genetically identical, sac-like polyps, these marine invertebrates secrete calcium carbonate to build the hard skeletons behind the world's tropical reefs — name them?
Coral are colonial marine invertebrates within the subphylum Anthozoa of the phylum Cnidaria.
Nicknamed for the material that made up most of its airframe, this British twin-engined combat aircraft of World War II was one of the fastest operational planes of 1941. What aircraft is this?
De Havilland Mosquito was a British twin-engined, multi-role combat aircraft, introduced during the Second World War.
Best known for a single spiky, strong-smelling fruit beloved across Southeast Asia, this plant genus also includes eight other species with edible fruit — which genus?
Durio is a genus of plants in the family Malvaceae.
With a US prevalence of about 8.2 cases per million births, this inherited disorder can cause complications from esophageal narrowing to skin cancer to amputation — which condition?
Epidermolysis bullosa (EB) is a group of rare medical conditions that result in easy blistering of the skin and mucous membranes.

Discovered in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb in 1952 and named for a pioneer of nuclear physics, element 100 is the heaviest that neutron bombardment can produce. Which synthetic element is it?
Fermium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Fm and atomic number 100.

This genus of scented flowering shrubs in the coffee family was named for an 18th-century naturalist, though Carl Linnaeus gets most of the credit over the botanist who first proposed it — which genus?
Gardenia is a genus of flowering plants in the coffee family, Rubiaceae, native to the tropical and subtropical regions of Africa, Asia, Madagascar, Pacific Islands, and Australia.

Descended from medieval hunting dogs once used to take down bears, wild boar, and deer, and later kept as guardians by German nobility, this breed is one of the two largest dog breeds in the world — name it?
Great Dane is a German breed of large mastiff-sighthound, which descends from hunting dogs of the Middle Ages used to hunt bears, wild boar, and deer.
Named by Linnaeus after the mythical strongman Heracles, this genus of towering herbs in the carrot family includes hogweed and cow parsnip — what is it?
Heracleum (plant) is a genus of biennial and perennial herbs in the carrot family Apiaceae.
Related to the sodium and calcium compounds found in household bleach, this chlorine-based oxidizer also occurs naturally as part of the human immune system. What is it?
Hypochlorous acid is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula ClOH, also written as HClO, HOCl, or ClHO.

Native to the tropical Americas but now planted worldwide, this flowering plant genus of 49 species has one member so widely introduced it's considered an environmental weed on five continents — what genus is it?
Jacaranda is a genus of 49 species of flowering plants in the family Bignoniaceae, native to tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas while cultivated around the world.
This Mexican-American astronaut flew on STS-128, led a branch at Johnson Space Center, and — urged on by President Obama — ran for Congress in 2012; who is he?
José M. Hernández (born August 7, 1962) is a Mexican-American engineer and astronaut.
Depicted as the goddess Minerva, this Italian physicist became the first woman with a science doctorate and the first salaried female university teacher. Who was she?
Laura Bassi (29 October 1711 - 20 February 1778) was an Italian physicist and academic.

This American single-engine supersonic interceptor, designed by Kelly Johnson after interviewing Korean War fighter pilots, became part of the 'Century Series' and was widely used as a Cold War fighter-bomber. What is it?
Lockheed F-104 Starfighter is an American single-engine, supersonic interceptor. It was also produced under license by other nations and saw widespread service outside the United States.
A large canine of South America resembling a red fox in markings but being neither fox nor wolf. It's the only species in its genus and the largest canine in South America. What is it?
Maned wolf (Chrysocyon brachyurus) is a large canine of South America.
Named in 1925 as an abbreviation of its chemical structure, this essential amino acid is required to kick-start protein synthesis — which amino acid is this?
Methionine (symbol Met or M) is an essential amino acid in humans.
Sitting just above the lip and under the nose, this style of facial hair on men has come in countless shapes across the centuries — what's it called?
Moustache is a growth of facial hair grown above the upper lip and under the nose of men.
Also called niacin, this organic compound is an essential vitamin B3 that plants and animals produce from the amino acid tryptophan. What is it?
Nicotinic acid is an organic compound and a vitamer of vitamin B3, an essential human nutrient.
This specialized subunit within a biological cell performs a specific function, and may be enclosed in its own membrane or exist without one. What is it?
Organelle is a specialized subunit, within a biological cell, that has a specific function.
Known in the US as a goober and in the UK as a monkey nut, this Fabaceae crop hides its edible seeds in underground pods. What is it?

Peanut (Arachis hypogaea), also known as the groundnut, goober (US, via Kikongo), goober pea, pindar (US, via Kikongo) or monkey nut (UK), is a legume crop grown mainly for its edible seeds, contained in underground pods.
Native to Chile and Peru and cultivated since Inca times, this nightshade fruit is known in English as the Cape gooseberry or goldenberry — what is its scientific name?
Physalis peruviana is a species of plant in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) native to Chile and Peru.
A strongly alkaline, water-soluble salt of carbonic acid, which compound with the formula K2CO3 is used in glassmaking and Dutch-process chocolate?
Potassium carbonate is the inorganic compound with the formula K2CO3. It is deliquescent, often appearing as a damp or wet solid.
Powered by a supermassive black hole accreting gas at its center, this extremely luminous type of galactic nucleus can outshine an entire galaxy thousands of times over. What is it?
Quasar is an extremely luminous active galactic nucleus (AGN).
He'd spent years building and selling theremins toward a Cornell physics PhD before unveiling, in 1964, the first commercial instrument of its kind — which American electronics pioneer was this?
Robert Moog (MOHG; May 23, 1934 - August 21, 2005) was an American electronics engineer and electronic music pioneer.
This condition gives the spine an irregular S- or C-shaped curve with a twist, and is often compared with kyphosis and lordosis — what is it?
Scoliosis (pl.: scolioses) is a medical condition in which the spine has an irregular curve in the coronal plane, associated with a rotational component.
This vertebrate organ system serves three main functions, protection, regulation, and sensation, and in mammals is made of multiple layers of ectodermal tissue. What is it?

Skin is the layer of usually soft, flexible outer tissue covering the body of a vertebrate animal, with three main functions: protection, regulation, and sensation. The adjective cutaneous means "of the skin" (from Latin cutis 'skin').
Named from the Greek word for tallow, this soft waxy 18-carbon saturated fatty compound is common in animal fats like beef tallow and lard — what is it called?
Stearic acid (stee-) is a saturated fatty acid with an 18-carbon chain.
Found naturally in grapes and other fruits, this crystalline compound's potassium salt is better known as cream of tartar, a key ingredient in homemade baking powder — which compound?
Tartaric acid is a white, crystalline organic acid that occurs naturally in many fruits, most notably in grapes but also in tamarinds, bananas, avocados, and citrus.
Joining Bethesda Game Studios in 1994, this video game director has since led development of both The Elder Scrolls and Fallout series, as well as 2023's Starfield. Who is he?
Todd Howard (born 1970) is an American video game designer, director, and producer who serves as director and executive producer at Bethesda Game Studios.
Native to boreal forests and Arctic tundra across the Northern Hemisphere, this small evergreen heath-family shrub produces edible berries central to Nordic cuisine — what plant is it?
Vaccinium vitis-idaea is a small evergreen shrub in the heath family, Ericaceae. It is known colloquially as the lingonberry, partridgeberry, foxberry, mountain cranberry, or cowberry.
A physician and Royal Society charter member, he surveyed confiscated Irish land for Cromwell's soldiers but is best remembered for pioneering 'political arithmetic' in economics — who was he?
William Petty (26 May 1623 - 16 December 1687) was an English economist, physician, scientist and philosopher.
This American psychologist devised a pyramid-shaped theory of human needs culminating in self-actualization, and was later ranked the 10th most-cited psychologist of the 20th century — who is he?

First flown as a stretched derivative of a popular narrow-body jet family in 1994, this twin-engine airliner carries up to 239 passengers and later gained a fuel-efficient 'neo' version with new winglets — which aircraft?
Airbus A321: Airliner, stretched model of the A320 family.
Native to Europe, Western Asia, and North Africa, this flowering plant lent its name — and originally its root — to a fluffy campfire treat, and is used in herbal medicine — which plant?
Its name comes from Latin words meaning 'to strangle' and 'chest,' and it describes pain caused by reduced blood flow to the heart muscle — what is this condition called?
Angina: Chest discomfort due to disorder of the heart muscles.

Once mistaken for bacteria, this domain of single-celled organisms is now known to be the group from which eukaryotes evolved, distinguished by ether-linked cell membranes and a unique whip-like motility structure. What domain is it?
Archaea: Domain of organisms. Traditionally, Archaea included only its prokaryotic members, but has since been found to be paraphyletic, as eukaryotes are known to have evolved from archaea.
Affecting roughly one in five people at some point and usually starting in childhood, this long-term itchy, red, cracked-skin condition is also simply called eczema — what's its formal name?
Atopic dermatitis: Long-term form of skin inflammation.
Second only to the capybara among living rodents and able to top 50 kg, this animal sports chisel-like incisors, webbed back feet, and a flat, scaly tail — what is it?
This class of aquatic molluscs — including clams, oysters, mussels, and scallops — has no head and encloses its soft body in a hinged pair of shells called valves — which class?
Bivalvia: Class of molluscs. The shell of a bivalve is composed of calcium carbonate, and consists of two, usually similar, parts called valves.
Named in honor of physicist Satyendra Nath Bose and coined by Paul Dirac, this class of subatomic particle has integer spin and includes force carriers like gluons and the Higgs — what is it called?
Boson: Class of subatomic particle. In particle physics, a boson is a subatomic particle whose spin quantum number has an integer value (0, 1, 2,...).

Made up largely of the gluteus maximus — the largest muscle in the human body — these two rounded parts of the posterior pelvic region sit between the lower back and the perineum, and have long served as a target for corporal punishment?
Buttocks: Anatomical feature on the posterior of some primates.
Native to Africa, the Middle East, and arid parts of Asia, this nocturnal, secretive wild cat is built for the chase with long legs and dramatically long tufted ears — which animal?
A Turkish geologist honored by academies from the US to Russia to Serbia, he received the Gustav-Steinmann-Medaille, geology's top German prize. Who is he?
Celâl Şengör: Turkish scientist, geologist. Ali Mehmet Celâl Şengör (Turkish: [ˈali ˈmehmet ˈdʒeɫal ˈʃænɟœɾ]; born 24 March 1955) is a Turkish geologist.
Once common as the refrigerant "Freon," these carbon-chlorine-fluorine compounds were phased out under the Montreal Protocol for chewing through the ozone layer — what are they?

Medieval German miners cursed an ore that looked metal-rich but smelted into nothing useful, naming it after a mischievous goblin — yet for centuries its blue pigment tinted glass and jewelry. Which element, symbol Co, atomic number 27, earned that goblin's name?
Cobalt: Chemical element with atomic number 27 (Co)

Known to NATO by the reporting name 'Mop' and to Canadian forces as the Canso, this WWII flying boat served every branch of the U.S. military and remained in some air forces into the 1980s — which aircraft?
Consolidated PBY Catalina: American 1930s flying boat.
Native to the Irano-Turanian region, this flowering plant's dried seeds season cuisines worldwide, despite no strong evidence backing its use in traditional medicine — which spice?
Cumin: Species of plant with seeds used as a spice.
Often tied to diseases like Alzheimer's, this incurable, progressive syndrome erodes memory, language, and motivation in stages — which condition is being described?
Spanning some 40 species from oceanic to river-dwelling and ranging down to a human-sized 1.7 meters, these toothed whales are kin to belugas and porpoises — what are they?
Dolphin: Informal classification of marine mammals, closely related to whales and porpoises.
This American astronomer proved that many so-called nebulae were actually separate galaxies, and in 1929 showed that galaxies recede faster the farther away they are — who is he?
Triggered by the parasympathetic nervous system and a rise in nitric oxide, this physiological event leaves an organ firm and engorged — what is it?
Erection: Physiological phenomenon involving the hardening and enlargement of the penis.

Also known as the wisent, this species is the heaviest wild land mammal on its continent — hunted to extinction in the wild by the early 20th century before being restored through captive breeding programs. Which animal?
European bison: Eurasian species of mammal. It is one of two extant species of bison, alongside the American bison.
This genus of about 850 tropical tree, shrub, and vine species is best known for two cultivated fruit-bearing members and serves as a vital food source for wildlife across the tropics — which genus?
Ficus: Genus of flowering plants in the mulberry family Moraceae.
Before becoming Ferrari's Formula One team principal in 2023, this Frenchman co-founded a junior-racing outfit that won back-to-back titles with Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg — who is he?
Combining Greek words for 'earth,' 'form,' and 'study,' what field examines how landscapes and seafloor features form and evolve over time?
This waterfowl family member is smaller than a swan but larger than a duck; its young are called goslings, and a flock on the ground is known as a gaggle — what bird is it?
Goose: Common name for a group of waterfowl.
This North Atlantic member of the true cod family is prized smoked as Finnan haddie or the Arbroath smokie — what fish is it?
Haddock: Species of fish. The haddock (Melanogrammus aeglefinus) is a saltwater ray-finned fish from the family Gadidae, the true cods.

Many people show no symptoms after catching this liver-attacking virus, but when signs do appear weeks later they can include nausea, yellowing skin, and fatigue — and an infection lasting past six months is deemed chronic. What is it?
Which of these counts as an accessory organ of digestion rather than part of the gut tube itself?
The accessory organs -- tongue, salivary glands, pancreas, liver and gallbladder -- feed into digestion without food passing through them.

This crystalline mineral form of frozen water occurs naturally on Earth, other planets, and even in Oort cloud objects, and has at least nineteen known phases depending on temperature and pressure — what is it?
Ice: Frozen water; the solid state of water.
Awarded the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physics, this British scientist discovered in 1897 that cathode rays were made of what we now call electrons — who is he?
Credited with popularizing the index fund, this investor founded The Vanguard Group and preached long-term patience over speculation — who is he?
John C. Bogle: American investor and business magnate (1929–2019)
Marketed as Nizoral, this antifungal medication also treats Cushing's syndrome and excess hair growth in women, though oral use risks liver damage — which drug?
This probability principle explains why a casino might lose money on a single spin of roulette but reliably earns a predictable percentage over many thousands of spins. What is it called?
Law of large numbers: Averages of repeated trials converge to the expected value.
Instrumental in the discovery of nuclear fission, this Austrian-Swedish physicist fled Nazi Germany in 1938 after losing her post under the Nuremberg Laws — who is she?
This American biologist argued that cells with nuclei arose from symbiotic mergers of bacteria, and co-developed the Gaia hypothesis with James Lovelock — who was she?

Originally hoping to become an engineer, this Italian physician became one of the first women to graduate from medical school in Italy and later devised an influential educational philosophy — who is she?
Maria Montessori: Italian physician and educator (1870–1952)
Comprising 18 to 24 species that hybridize freely where their ranges overlap, this genus of the mint family thrives in wet, moist soils worldwide — what is it?
Mentha: Genus of flowering plants in the family Lamiaceae.
NATO nicknames it 'Foxhound,' and at roughly 3,000 km/h it's the fastest operational combat aircraft known — which interceptor, a Soviet successor to the MiG-25, is it?
Mikoyan MiG-31: Interceptor aircraft. The MiG-31 is the fastest known operational combat aircraft, with a top speed around 3,000 km/h (1,600 knots).
Grown to feed silkworms for commercial silk production, this fast-growing tree releases its pollen at more than half the speed of sound — which species?
Morus alba: Plant species in the fig family.

The males of this stocky Arctic cetacean sport a spiralled 'tusk' up to three metres long — actually a protruding left canine tooth thought to work as a weapon, a tool, and maybe a salinity sensor. What animal is it?

Usually made from unleavened dough that's rolled, cut, or extruded into long strips, this staple food is called pasta in Italian cuisine and split into wheat-based and starch-based varieties in Chinese cooking — what is it?
Noodle: Staple food made from unleavened dough, commonly long and thin.
Discovered by naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace in 1859, this fungus hijacks carpenter ants' brains and marches them down to the forest floor before killing them — which organism?

Ophiocordyceps unilateralis: Species of fungus. Ophiocordyceps unilateralis, commonly known as zombie-ant fungus, is an insect-pathogenic fungus, discovered by the British naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace in 1859.
First domesticated in Mesoamerica and led in production today by India, this tropical fruit belongs to the small genus Carica — what is it?
Papaya: Species of tropical fruit plant.
Known for its speed, this large crow-sized raptor has a blue-grey back, barred white underparts, and a black head — an avivore with marked sexual dimorphism — what is it?
Peregrine falcon: Fastest known animal and common bird of prey.
Named after the Latin word for the magpie, a bird known for its opportunistic feeding habits, this eating disorder involves craving non-food objects — what is it?
Pica (disorder): Compulsive eating of non-food items.
Nicknamed the 'terror of Bengal' for choking waterways across the world, this South American aquatic plant is commonly known as water hyacinth — what is its scientific name?
Pontederia crassipes: Aquatic plant native to the Amazon basin.

Marketed under brand names like Sudafed, this nasal decongestant can act as a stimulant and appetite suppressant at higher doses, making it both a medicine-cabinet staple and, at times, a drug of abuse. What is it?
Pseudoephedrine: Synthetic decongestant. Pseudoephedrine is a sympathomimetic medication which is used as a nasal decongestant to treat nasal congestion.
Colorless and odorless, this radioactive noble gas with atomic number 86 is a decay product of radium and eventually settles into stable isotopes of lead?
Radon: Chemical element with atomic number 86 (Rn)
Made up of 12 paired bones plus the sternum and spine, this bony enclosure of the chest shields the heart and lungs while housing the muscles used for breathing — what is it?
Rib cage: Bone structure of the thorax.
Originally conceived as a jet trainer before its role expanded to supersonic strike and reconnaissance, this Anglo-French attack aircraft is today flown only by the Indian Air Force. What is it?
SEPECAT Jaguar: French/British attack aircraft. It was also later license produced by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited in India for use of the Indian Air Force.
After early family-friendly Christian games found little success, which developer switched to horror in 2014 and created a hit franchise of horror video games?
Scott Cawthon: American video game developer (born 1978)

Adapted from the Army's Black Hawk with folding rotor blades and a hinged tail to fit aboard ships, this twin-engine Navy helicopter handles everything from anti-submarine warfare to medical evacuation — which aircraft?
The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom
Sikorsky SH-60 Seahawk: Naval helicopter series of the H-60/S-70 family.
Native to the tropical Americas and a cousin of the cherimoya, which spiny fruit smells like pineapple and tastes like strawberries and apple with a sour citrus tang?
Soursop: Tropical fruit tree. Soursop (also called graviola, guyabano, and in Hispanic America guanábana) is the fruit of Annona muricata, a broadleaf, flowering, evergreen tree.

These long-legged wading birds communicate by clattering their bills rather than calling, favor drier habitats than their heron cousins, and are collectively known as a 'muster' or a 'phalanx' — which birds?
Sold under the brand name Cialis, this erectile dysfunction medication can remain effective for up to 36 hours after a single dose — which drug?
Tadalafil: Medication used to treat erectile dysfunction.
Native to the tropical Americas, this small evergreen tree's fermented seeds become cocoa powder, cocoa butter, and chocolate — which tree?
Theobroma cacao: Species of tree grown for its seeds.

Though most often viral, this throat condition turns into the dreaded 'strep throat' when group A streptococcus is to blame, and can leave you with a sore throat, fever, and swollen glands — what is it?
Developed by Microsoft, this open-source language layers optional static typing onto JavaScript and transpiles back into it for use on both browsers and servers — what is it?
TypeScript: Programming language and superset of JavaScript.
This legume, also called the broad bean, can trigger a dangerous reaction called favism in people with a certain metabolic blood disorder — what species is it?
Vicia faba: Species of plant in the pea and bean family.
One of the widest-ranging mammals on Earth, this adaptable suid native to Eurasia and North Africa has turned invasive wherever people introduced it — what is it?
This French mathematician and physicist wrote Institutions de Physique, a work translated into German and Italian that sparked heated 18th-century debate — who is she?
Émilie du Châtelet: French mathematician, physicist, and author (1706–1749)
Lawrencium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for lawrencium is Lr. Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lr and atomic number 103.

Paul Lynde is a comedian. Paul Edward Lynde (June 13, 1926 – January 10, 1982) was an American comedian, actor, and game-show panelist.
In what year was Will Poulter born?
Will Poulter: William Jack Poulter (born 28 January 1993) is an English actor.

Brittany Murphy: Murphy was born in Atlanta; her parents, Angelo Bertolotti and Sharon Murphy, divorced when she was three years old.
In what year was Howard Hughes born?
Howard Hughes: Howard Robard Hughes Jr. (December 24, 1905 – April 5, 1976) was an American aviator, aerospace engineer, business magnate, film producer, and investor.
In what year was Aubrey Plaza born?
Aubrey Plaza: Aubrey Christina Plaza (born June 26, 1984) is an American actress, comedian, writer, and producer.
In what year was Sofía Vergara born?
Sofía Vergara: Sofía Margarita Vergara Vergara (Spanish: [soˈfi.a βeɾˈɣaɾa]; born July 10, 1972) is a Colombian and American actress and television personality.
In what year was Robin Wright born?
Robin Wright: Robin Gayle Wright (born April 8, 1966) is an American actress, producer and director.
In what year was Meghan, Duchess of Sussex born?
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex: Meghan was born and raised in Los Angeles, California.
In what year was Jennifer Lopez born?
Jennifer Lopez: Jennifer Lynn Lopez (born July 24, 1969) is an American singer, songwriter, actress, dancer, and businesswoman.

Ben Affleck: Benjamin Géza Affleck (born August 15, 1972) is an American actor and filmmaker.
In what year was Reneé Rapp born?
Reneé Rapp: Reneé Jane Rapp (born January 10, 2000) is an American singer-songwriter and actress.
In what year did Kirk Douglas die?
